claims.text: The Z method within ab initio molecular dynamics can calculate melting temperature, fusion entropy, fusion enthalpy, and volume change at melting.
The Z method is a computationally efficient alternative to full thermodynamic integration.
The target material is a high-melting refractory material initially in a crystalline solid state.
In the proposed Z-method simulation, an initially solid system is overheated under constant-energy NVE conditions until it spontaneously melts.
The Z method replaces the thermodynamic-integration step of the ab initio free-energy approach.
Solid and liquid phases can be identified within the same Z-method simulation run near the superheating limit.
The superheated crystalline lattice transforms into a liquid.
The melting transition produces a discontinuous jump in energy.
The melting transition produces a discontinuous change in volume.
Constant-energy Z-method dynamics place the material in a metastable superheated state.
Spontaneous melting occurs once a threshold energy is exceeded.
Analysis of the melting event's energy or enthalpy discontinuity yields the melting temperature and fusion enthalpy.
Fusion entropy can be derived from the quantities obtained during the Z-method melting event.
Analysis of the volume change during the melting event yields the volume change at melting.
Z-method melting properties will be comparable to values from full ab initio thermodynamic integration.
The Z method has significantly lower computational expense and is therefore more suitable for high-throughput screening.
Conventional ab initio thermodynamic-integration calculations are highly accurate but computationally expensive.
The proposed approach is expected to be valid for high-melting materials without extreme anharmonicity or complex multiphase transitions at melting.
Agreement between the Z method and thermodynamic integration may vary with chemical complexity and melting behavior, and reliability for some refractory high-entropy alloys remains unestablished.
Substantial disagreement with thermodynamic integration or failure to reproduce results across independent simulations would falsify the proposed viability of the Z method.

contradictions.description: The simulation is specified as constant-energy NVE, yet the hypothesis calls for an energy discontinuity or abrupt change in total energy during melting. Total energy is constrained in an NVE trajectory, so this observable is internally inconsistent unless the intended quantity is temperature, potential energy, or an energy comparison across separate trajectories.

NVE conventionally fixes volume, while the hypothesis proposes observing a volume jump within the same run and deriving the melting volume change from it. A separate variable-cell protocol, multiple fixed-volume calculations, or another ensemble would need to be specified.

The mechanism states that a threshold energy is exceeded under constant-energy conditions. Energy can be varied between separate NVE simulations, but it does not increase and cross a threshold during an individual constant-energy trajectory as currently worded.
